## From Learned Coordination to Agent Harnesses

The LLM wave did not invent multi-agent coordination. Classical multi-agent systems, or MAS, studied coordination among multiple autonomous actors through protocols, planning, negotiation, communication, markets, and distributed control. Multi-agent reinforcement learning, or MARL, studied one influential branch of that problem: how multiple learned policies interact through rewards, observations, actions, messages, centralized training, or environment state. Modern LLM-agent systems are different again. They mostly coordinate pretrained model calls at test time through prompts, tools, context windows, files, memories, code, browsers, APIs, logs, permissions, human review, and artifacts.

The older literature therefore matters as selective inheritance, not as a blueprint. Emergent-communication and MARL work showed that multiple agents, message channels, and shared objectives do not automatically produce useful coordination. Learned communication can be degenerate or uninterpretable; shared rewards do not solve credit assignment; and local success can fail to compose into global success [@rialdial; @commnet; @tarmac; @maddpg; @coma; @qmix; @mappo; @smac]. Larger-scale systems such as OpenAI Five and hide-and-seek autocurricula showed the promise of interaction and self-play, but also the dependence on restricted environments, simulator design, and large training infrastructure [@dota2; @emergenttooluse].

The continuity is not a term-by-term translation from MARL to LLM agents. It is a recurring coordination problem under a different implementation regime. Earlier work made clear that adding agents, messages, and shared objectives does not by itself produce reliable collective behavior. Modern LLM systems encounter that broad failure pattern through different mechanisms: context loss, stale summaries, duplicated work, weak verification, artifact corruption, unsafe tool use, and unclear attribution. The lesson is not that LLM multi-agent systems are MARL systems with text. It is that language and tools make coordination easier to express, but not automatically easier to make reliable.

The immediate precondition for modern multi-agent LLM systems was the transformation of an LLM call into an agentic worker: a loop that can observe, reason, act, call tools, retrieve state, write files, execute code, inspect results, and leave traces. ReAct made the reasoning-action-observation loop explicit [@react]. Later agent frameworks and environments made the loop programmable, inspectable, and evaluable across code, browsers, APIs, devices, and workplace tasks [@autogen; @agentscope; @magenticone; @openhands; @sweagent; @webarena; @osworld; @gaia; @taubench; @swebench]. @tbl-foundations-contrast makes the substrate shift explicit.

| Dimension | Pre-LLM MAS and MARL | Modern LLM multi-agent systems |
|---|---|---|
| Agent substrate | autonomous actors, protocols, or learned policies | prompted, tool-using workers |
| Coordination phase | protocol design, training-time coordination, or fixed policy execution | test-time orchestration |
| Communication medium | actions, rewards, learned signals, messages, environment state | language, structured messages, files, logs, artifacts |
| Diversity source | roles, protocols, policies, observations, rewards, or environment positions | models, prompts, roles, tools, contexts, memories, branches, verifiers, humans |
| Work product | agreement, allocation, reward, game outcome, task success | patches, tests, documents, reports, browser/API states, experiment logs |
| Failure surface | non-stationarity, credit assignment, protocol failure, local-global mismatch | context loss, weak verification, duplicated work, artifact corruption, merge failure, unsafe state propagation |

: Contrast between pre-LLM MAS/MARL and modern LLM multi-agent systems. Modern systems shift coordination from learned policies and protocols toward test-time orchestration over language, tools, files, logs, artifacts, and human review. {#tbl-foundations-contrast}

Once an LLM call became a stateful worker, multiplicity became useful in a different way. Modern multi-agent value usually comes from test-time diversity and allocation, not from end-to-end learned team policies. A system can spend inference on different prompts, models, tools, retrieval sources, memories, artifact branches, sampling paths, critics, verifiers, or human reviewers, then select or merge what survives evidence. This is why agent count is a weak descriptor: the causal question is what useful difference the extra worker introduced and how that difference was checked.

The practical consequence is that LLM multi-agent research should borrow the caution of older coordination work without inheriting its problem formulation wholesale. Useful multi-agent behavior still depends on how information, authority, and feedback are routed, but the routing problem now runs through tools, context, memory, artifacts, evaluators, and human attention.

This shift explains why the early wave so often produced simulated teams and societies. Language made coordination look solved at the interface level. A designer could write "manager," "engineer," "critic," or "scientist" into a prompt; give each worker tools and memory; and inspect a transcript that resembled human collaboration. That interface-level legibility made team-like systems natural. It also made the field vulnerable to confusing role description with reliable coordination.
